units.title: Attention shapes, prefill and decode reuse, and materialized traffic
outcomes: Derive attention shapes and leading matrix-multiply FLOPs for prefill and single-token decode.
Count score and probability storage separately from reads and writes.
Explain why decode has less query-side reuse without declaring it bandwidth-bound from shape alone.
units.why: The score matrix is often larger than the inputs. Its shape explains what tiling removes and why a prefill schedule need not work well for decode.

next.note: Remove the materialized matrices while preserving the attention equation.

study.title: FlashAttention, arXiv:2205.14135v2
study.locator: Section 2.2, Standard Attention Implementation, and Algorithm 0 (p. 4)

study.title: FlashInfer decode shape and layout contract
study.depth: Read the parameter contracts only. Do not implement the production dispatch yet.

focus: For batch size \(B\), query heads \(H_q\), query length \(L\), key length \(S\) and equal key/value head width \(d\), scores have shape \(B \times H_q \times L \times S\). Attention is \(O = \operatorname{softmax}(QK^\top/\sqrt{d})V\), with softmax over keys.

Count the two dense matrix products as \(4BH_qLSd\) FLOPs, counting each multiply-add as two. Scaling, masking and softmax are additional work. Prefill has many query rows; ordinary decode has one per request.

Algorithm 0 writes and reads both scores and probabilities. At \(b\) bytes per intermediate element this is \(4bBH_qLS\) requested bytes, not the complete kernel traffic or a hardware-counter measurement.
Decode can reuse each KV head across grouped query heads, but cannot reuse it across a long query tile. Layout, cache residency and schedule determine whether that reuse is realized.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, count noncausal MHA with \(B = 1\), \(H_q = 8\), \(L = S = 1024\), \(d = 64\), and two-byte score/probability storage. The two intermediates occupy 32 MiB and their write-read traffic is 64 MiB; the two matrix products require \(2{,}147{,}483{,}648\) FLOPs. For decode with \(L = 1\) and the same cache, one ideal read of keys and values is 2 MiB. Explain every excluded byte category.
traps: Calling storage size traffic. A tensor may be read several times, and actual memory transactions can exceed requested bytes.
Using the paper's unscaled equation as a different model. Its exposition omits the scale; your reference must include the model's scale.
Assuming the paper's HBM hardware. The same dataflow applies to GPUs with GDDR memory, but bandwidth and on-chip capacity differ.

selfTest.q: Does avoiding the score matrix remove quadratic prefill arithmetic?
selfTest.a: No. Dense attention still computes every allowed query-key interaction. Tiling changes storage and data movement, not the leading dense matrix-product count.

selfTest.q: Why are 32 MiB of intermediates responsible for 64 MiB of requested traffic in this model?
selfTest.a: Each of the two tensors is written once and read once. This excludes input/output movement, repeated tile loads, masks and workspace.

selfTest.q: Does a long KV cache prove decode is memory-bound?
selfTest.a: No. It predicts substantial KV movement. Launches, insufficient parallelism, reductions and address translation may dominate; timing and profiling must distinguish them.

practice.name: LeetGPU 6: Softmax Attention
practice.note: Implement the unchanged `solve` signature in CUDA or Triton. Use the public generators and reference in your own local harness; the repository lacks `core.challenge_base`, and `scripts/run_challenge.py` submits to a service with an API key rather than running locally. Recreate the generated tensors and compare outputs using the challenge's tolerances. The cases include rectangular attention and odd head widths. The section mini-project covers the traffic ledger.

units.stopWhen: Your traffic ledger reproduces the counts, and your attention implementation matches every functional case of challenge 6 without claiming a speedup.

fit.note: The primary paper supplies the traffic derivation, FlashInfer supplies decode shapes, and challenge 6 supplies bounded checked practice.

units.title: Online softmax state, query and key-value tiling and output tolerance
outcomes: Derive the running maximum, normalizer and weighted numerator invariants.
Implement a tiled forward pass that retains only query-tile state on chip.
Validate accumulation and rescaling with an independent reference and a stated extreme-value policy.
units.why: Online softmax lets a query row consume keys in pieces. Rescaling both the denominator and weighted numerator is what makes those pieces one attention operation.

next.note: Extend the tiled state to masked rows and shared KV heads.

study.title: Online Normalizer Calculation, arXiv:1805.02867v2
study.locator: Section 3, Algorithm 3 and its induction proof; Section 3.1, equations 3 and 4 (pp. 2 to 4)
study.depth: Stop before Section 4. The proof assumes finite logits; its associativity is a real-arithmetic statement, not bitwise floating-point equivalence.

study.title: CS336 Assignment 2: weighted sum and tiled forward
study.locator: Commit ca8bc81: Section 4.2.1, Example - Weighted Sum, forward pass (pp. 17 to 20); Section 4.2.2, Details of the FlashAttention forward pass and Algorithm 1 (pp. 24 to 25); problem `flash_forward` parts (a) and (b) (pp. 26 to 27)
study.depth: Read the weighted-sum forward example before attention; defer its backward kernel. Start with the public test sizes, not the B200 sweep. Add bounds checks beyond the handout's power-of-two contract.

focus: For processed keys, keep \(m = \max_j s_j\), \(\ell = \sum_j \exp(s_j-m)\) and \(u = \sum_j \exp(s_j-m)v_j\). Output is \(u/\ell\). A rising maximum changes the scale of all old contributions.
For new tile scores \(T\), use \(m' = \max(m,\max T)\), \(a = \exp(m-m')\), \(\ell' = a\ell + \sum_j \exp(T_j-m')\) and \(u' = au + \sum_j \exp(T_j-m')v_j\). Normalize once at the end.
Keep the query tile and row state while streaming key/value tiles. Accumulate reductions and weighted outputs in `tl.float32`; record dot-product precision and casts separately from output dtype.

For finite inputs, compare with a dense double-precision reference using absolute and relative error. Handle empty tiles explicitly. Define all-masked rows as zero output and negative-infinite logsumexp, or reject them; reject NaN and infinite unmasked logits unless you implement another policy.
units.reproduce: Without the source, merge two tiles with logits `torch.tensor([0., 1., 2., 3.], dtype=torch.float64)` and scalar values `torch.tensor([1., 2., 3., 4.], dtype=torch.float64)`, split after the second entry. In PyTorch 2.14.1 the weighted output is approximately 3.492652734585769. Then implement query/key tiling for seed 0 standard-normal inputs of shapes 2 by 17 by 7 and 2 by 19 by 7, with scale \(1/\sqrt{7}\). Both 4 by 5 and 8 by 8 tiles must match the double-precision dense reference within `rtol=1e-12, atol=1e-12` on CPU.
traps: Rescaling the denominator but leaving the old weighted numerator unchanged. A later larger maximum then changes the answer.
Padding keys with zero scores. They still receive probability mass; invalid keys must contribute neither to the normalizer nor the numerator.
Evaluating a difference of two negative infinities for an empty tile. Branch or use safe neutral-state handling rather than letting NaNs enter the recurrence.

selfTest.q: Why can you postpone normalization until the final tile?
selfTest.a: The numerator and denominator share the same running exponential scale. Their ratio is the normalized weighted sum over all keys processed so far.
For finite logits it is associative in exact real arithmetic: each state summarizes the same weighted exponential sums. Floating-point merge order can change rounding.

selfTest.q: Does subtracting the maximum solve every extreme-value case?
selfTest.a: No. It controls exponential overflow for finite scores, but cannot repair overflow in the dot product or define softmax of an all-masked row. Those need separate contracts.

practice.name: CS336 Assignment 2: `flash_forward` (a) and (b)
practice.locator: Connect both attention classes through `tests/adapters.py`; run `pytest tests/test_attention.py -k test_flash_forward_pass` after adding causal support in the next unit
practice.note: First pass the PyTorch case and the noncausal Triton case. The public inputs use batch size 4, sequence length 128 and head width 64, and compare output and saved logsumexp with `rtol=1e-2, atol=1e-2`. They do not check tails or extremes. Add those in `kernellab`; do not reuse the tiled algorithm as its own oracle.

units.stopWhen: You derive the two-state merge, pass both noncausal forward tests, and your own partial-tile and extreme-finite tests pass a justified error budget.

fit.note: The online-normalizer proof and CS336 forward algorithm cover derivation and implementation, with public tests and mini-project edge tests. TensorTonic's client-rendered statement was not verifiable, so CS336 is the checked practice route.
